grammarOverrides.from: French pour can identify a beneficiary (ce livre est pour Ana) or purpose (j’étudie pour apprendre). Par can describe a route through a place (nous passons par le parc) and occurs in merci pour ton aide. A cause often needs à cause de (fermé à cause de la pluie), rather than par. For heading toward a place without promising arrival, use vers: je me dirige vers la bibliothèque.
grammarOverrides.to: French pour can identify a beneficiary (ce livre est pour Ana) or purpose (j’étudie pour apprendre). Par can describe a route through a place (nous passons par le parc). Pour also occurs in merci pour ton aide. A cause often needs à cause de (fermé à cause de la pluie), rather than par. For heading toward a place without promising arrival, use vers: je me dirige vers la bibliothèque.

cautionOverrides.from: The English source explicitly says the learner used to study Spanish, so l’espagnol remains the subject of that line. French imparfait is not a word-for-word copy of Spanish imperfect forms; examples use natural French. For a single completed event, use the passé composé taught in Core 26.
cautionOverrides.to: Use the imparfait for repeated past habits and the passé composé for a single completed event. The French-course example is “J’étudiais le français l’après-midi.”

cautionOverrides.from: Spanish por/para are not a universal two-word French map. The source’s “because of the rain” becomes à cause de la pluie, while “toward the library” becomes vers la bibliothèque. English “through / because of” is pinned as a source gloss, but par by itself does not cover every because-of case; the French card includes a contextual note.
cautionOverrides.to: Pour expresses beneficiary or purpose; par can express a route. Use à cause de for the rain in this lesson and vers for heading toward a place. The broad “through / because of” source gloss is split into contextual French expressions.
cautionOverrides.reason: Remove Spanish-only comparison and preserve contextual distinction
